q: What is pre-training and why is it self-supervised?
short: Training a base model to predict the next token over a huge unlabelled corpus; the targets are the text's own next tokens, so no human labels are needed.
mistakes: Calling it supervised learning with labels.

q: Causal vs masked language modelling?
short: Causal LMs predict each token from the left context only (GPT, Llama) and can generate; masked LMs predict hidden tokens using both sides (BERT), better for understanding but not free generation.

q: Describe the pre-training data pipeline.
short: Collect (web, books, code), clean and filter (boilerplate, low quality, toxic, personal data), deduplicate (exact and near), tokenize, then train on the shuffled token stream.

q: Why is deduplication important?
short: Repeated text makes the model memorise rather than generalise, wastes compute, inflates benchmark scores through leakage, and raises the risk of regurgitating private or copyrighted text.

q: How does BPE build a vocabulary?
short: Start from characters or bytes and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token until the vocabulary reaches the target size.

q: What is continuous pre-training?
short: Continuing next-token training of a base model on domain text (medical, legal, code) to add domain knowledge cheaply while keeping general ability.
mistakes: Using a high learning rate and forgetting general skills.

q: What do scaling laws say?
short: Test loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute when the others aren't limiting, so performance at large scale can be predicted from small runs.

q: Apply the Chinchilla rule to a 70B model.
Why is C ≈ 6ND?
short: Each parameter does about 2 FLOPs per token in the forward pass (multiply and add) and about 4 in the backward pass (gradients w.r.t. activations and weights), so ~6 FLOPs per parameter per token.
detail: Ignores attention's n² term for moderate context.

q: Compute the Jaccard similarity of two near-duplicate sentences.
short: Split each into 3-word shingles: 'quick brown fox jumps…' vs '…fox leaps…' share 4 of 10 distinct shingles, J = 0.40; flagged at a 0.3 threshold.
detail: One word change breaks k shingles.

q: Why might a team train a model with far more than 20 tokens per parameter?
short: Chinchilla optimises training compute only; inference cost scales with N, so a smaller model trained longer is cheaper to serve for the same quality, which pays off when the model answers billions of queries.

q: How do you avoid catastrophic forgetting during continuous pre-training?
short: Lower learning rate with warm-up, mix in general data (replay), monitor general benchmarks alongside domain ones, and limit the number of domain tokens/epochs.
detail: Data mixture is the main lever.
follow: How to choose the replay ratio?

q: How do tokenizers affect cost and behaviour?
short: Tokens per word vary by language and domain, so some languages cost more and fit less in context; splitting numbers and rare names into odd pieces explains weaknesses like letter counting or arithmetic.

q: What does a masked LM train on and why is that less sample-efficient?
short: Only the masked positions (~15%) provide targets per pass, whereas a causal LM gets a target at every position.

q: What makes data 'high quality' for pre-training?
short: Well-formed, informative, diverse and deduplicated text, filtered for spam, boilerplate, toxicity and personal data, with a deliberate mixture of domains (code, maths, multilingual).

q: You have a fixed compute budget of 10²³ FLOPs. How do you choose model size and data?
short: Fit scaling curves on small runs, find the loss-optimal N for C = 6ND (on the order of 10–30B parameters with ~0.5–1T+ tokens, depending on the fit), then shift toward a smaller N trained longer if inference volume is high; check data availability and repeat limits.
mistakes: Choosing the largest model that fits.

q: Why are scaling laws useful despite being empirical?
short: They make performance predictable across orders of magnitude, letting teams compare architectures and data choices on small runs, pick hyper-parameters and budget large runs; but they hold only within the regime measured and for the loss, not every downstream skill.

q: Design a near-duplicate detection stage for a 10-billion-document crawl.
short: Normalise text, hash for exact dups, compute MinHash signatures over word shingles, use locality-sensitive hashing to find candidate pairs above a Jaccard threshold, cluster and keep one per cluster; also dedup against benchmark test sets.
detail: Tune k and threshold on samples.

q: What happens when you run out of unique high-quality data?
short: Repeating data for a few epochs is nearly as good as new data, but returns diminish with many repeats; options include multilingual and code data, better filtering of lower tiers, and carefully filtered synthetic data.

q: CPT vs RAG for a legal-domain assistant?
short: CPT bakes domain language and knowledge into the weights (helps style, terminology, reasoning) but is costly and goes stale; RAG retrieves current documents at query time with citations. Often combine: CPT or fine-tune for fluency, RAG for facts.
mistakes: Using CPT to keep facts up to date.
